The Old Woman

I looked for the title of the tune, as Beethoven did arrange it, and didn’t find it either here or on Tunearch, so I’ve transcribed the tune directly from Clinton (no. 26) except for the fermatas. The title might be easily confused with either “The Merry Old Woman” or “Get Up Old Woman And Shake Yourself,” but the tune seems to be neither of these.

↳ Posted by NylonFlute on February 10th, 2022.

The Old Woman, X:5

Version arranged by Beethoven in Beethoven’s 12 Irish Songs, WoO 154, no. 3 under the title “The Farewell Song.”

Lyrics by William Smyth (1765 - 1849):

O Erin! To thy harp divine
I bid adieu:
Yet let me now its sounds resign
With homage due.
Thy gen’rous sons, that know not fear,
Their feelings, genius, fire:
O blest be all! But Erin dear,
Be blest thy lyre.

O where the heart that would not bound
With answering beat,
To hear thy Planxty’s dancing sound,
And numbers sweet.
And where the heart that sinks not low,
And musing melts away,
To hear thy harp’s deep lonely flow,
When mourns the lay.

No toil can e’er such sweets supply
No chymic power,
As brings me bee, with honied thigh,
From wild heath flower:
And Science, that could wake the strings
To chords of rapture high.
May envy, while she smiling sings
Thy minstrelsy.

↳ Posted by birlibirdie on March 12th, 2022.

The Shan Van Vocht, X:6

This version of An tSean Bhean Bhocht is taken from Seán Ó Riada’s recording (Ó Riada’s Farewell - https://thesession.org/recordings/1821). He plays it as a slow air, then as a one part (unswung) hornpipe. The sleeve notes say it was used as an air for the song of the same name, where the Poor Old Woman represents Ireland. The first verse is given as:
O! The French are on the say,
says the Shan Van Vocht,
The French are on the say,
Says the Shan Van Vocht
O! The French are in the bay
They’ll be here without delay
And the orange will decay,
Says the Shan Van Vocht

Interestingly Seán Ó Baoill in his sleeve notes says, that in the Gaelic songs, the SBB is never anything but a an Old Woman of the Roads.
The tune was published by Bunting in 1809 and can be seen on ITMA
https://www.itma.ie/digital-library/score/bunting-vol-2-31
This has some similarities to Ó Riada’s except in a bouncy 6/8 rhythm (and in B flat, and 28 bars, and parts of the melody…). The same air was used by Thomas Moore for his poem “Loves Young Dream”. Unsurprisingly the setting is very close to Bunting’s and almost identical to Nylon Flute’s X:5 (which I think is from Beethoven, who I guess got it indirectly from Bunting?) These settings have unusual numbers of bars (20 for Moore - except he added on 4 rest bars for the singer) which would make it feel like a set dance.

In fact Ó Riada’s setting is closer to X:3, the first tune. Indeed it is even more similar to John O Leary’s version. These settings are simpler and shorter (8 bars) than the presumed source - Bunting’s. Of course this would make the tune more suitable for dancing down in Munster. So did JOL get it from SOR or vice versa. Or was the air around in Sliabh Luachra before both of them, even before Bunting?
The song seems to be sung to a different air these days. (I’ll post that later)

↳ Posted by brailsford on October 23rd, 2022.

The Shan Van Vocht, X:7

This is the air of the song An tSeanbhean Bhocht from West Kerry (Muireann Nic Amhlaoibh and friends). Its resemblance to the Ó Riada setting is only slight (same 8 bars and three accented beats on 2nd, 4th and 8th bar - the attached setting X:7 de-emphasises the crotchets because its based on the instrumental break). https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fttJFNc-Wwg
(Normally I reckon a significantly different tune requires a separate entry on The Session, but I feel this tune is best set down here.)

For yet another air plus lyrics where the SBB is clearly not standing in for Ireland, listen to this version from Donegal by Ríoghnach Connolly:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=endZFqb6wh4

Finally, there are two other airs collected by A Martin Freeman (probably from West Cork around Ballyvourney in the 1920)
https://www.itma.ie/digital-library/score/freeman-66
https://www.itma.ie/digital-library/score/freeman-65
called Shan Van Voght and An Shaunvean Vocht. These bear no resemblance to any of the settings here. Intriguingly Ó Riada was familiar with Freeman’s collection; he lectured on him and lived nearby in Cúil Aodha.

↳ Posted by brailsford on October 23rd, 2022.

Re: The Shan Van Vocht / The Poor Old Woman

There are two settings in O’Neill’s Music of Ireland called The Poor Old Woman (# 324 and #325). The first is broadly similar to X:2 and X:6. The second is similar in length but, to my ears anyway, a bit odd!
